claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and the current experimental results.

claims.claim: Perturbing activity of sensory neurons during the locomotor CP causes lasting changes to behaviour.
claims.source: This result also supports previous work that showed perturbing activity of sensory neurons during the locomotor CP causes lasting changes to behaviour (Fushiki et al., 2013; Carreira-Rosario et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Fushiki et al., 2013 and Carreira-Rosario et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Ch neuron activation provided a complete rescue of both network and cellular-level phenotypes associated with embryonic exposure to PTX.
claims.source: Remarkably, ch neuron activation provided a complete rescue of both network and cellular-level phenotypes associated with embryonic exposure to PTX.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the rescue data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claims.claim: Recovery from electroshock following exposure to PTX was rescued to control levels when PTX was paired with ch neuron activation (72.03 ± 5.71 s, EtOH; 194.7 ± 12.22 s, PTX; 92.75 ± 8.95 s, PTX + Ch; n = 40, 40, 40; p<0.0001 for EtOH vs. PTX and PTX vs. PTX vs. PTX + Ch, 0.58 for EtOH vs. PTX + Ch).
claims.source: Thus, recovery from electroshock, which was again increased following exposure to PTX, was rescued to control levels when PTX was paired with ch neuron activation (72.03 ± 5.71 s, EtOH; 194.7 ± 12.22 s, PTX; 92.75 ± 8.95 s, PTX + Ch; n = 40, 40, 40; p<0.0001 for EtOH vs. PTX and PTX vs. PTX vs. PTX + Ch, 0.58 for EtOH vs. PTX + Ch) (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: PTX-induced increase in synchrony of activity between adjacent aCC motoneurons was rescued by ch neuron activation (0.96 ± 0.07 s, EtOH; 0.63 ± 0.06 s, PTX; 0.88 ± 0.08 s, PTX + Ch; n = 27, 28, 27; p=0.004 for EtOH vs. PTX, 0.75 for EtOH vs. PTX + Ch, 0.03 for PTX vs. PTX + Ch).
claims.source: PTX-induced increase in synchrony of activity between adjacent aCC motoneurons was also rescued (0.96 ± 0.07 s, EtOH; 0.63 ± 0.06 s, PTX; 0.88 ± 0.08 s, PTX + Ch; n = 27, 28, 27; p=0.004 for EtOH vs. PTX, 0.75 for EtOH vs. PTX + Ch, 0.03 for PTX vs. PTX + Ch) (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The increased strength of excitatory A18a inputs to aCC following exposure to PTX was rescued by stimulation of ch neurons during the CP (12.92 ± 1.704 Hz, EtOH; 22.79 ± 2.42 Hz, PTX; 14.75 ± 1.98 s, PTX + Ch; n = 8, 8, 8; p=0.008 for EtOH vs PTX, 0.53 for EtOH vs. PTX + Ch, 0.023 for PTX vs. PTX + Ch).
claims.source: Finally, the increased strength of excitatory A18a inputs to aCC following exposure to PTX was rescued by stimulation of ch neurons during the CP (12.92 ± 1.704 Hz, EtOH; 22.79 ± 2.42 Hz, PTX; 14.75 ± 1.98 s, PTX + Ch; n = 8, 8, 8; p=0.008 for EtOH vs PTX, 0.53 for EtOH vs. PTX + Ch, 0.023 for PTX vs. PTX + Ch) (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: CPs integrate the excitatory and inhibitory activity to which they are exposed, to compute a sum that leads to a corresponding output in the mature locomotor network.
claims.source: These results support the hypothesis that CPs integrate the excitatory and inhibitory activity to which they are exposed, to compute a sum that leads to a corresponding output in the mature locomotor network.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the rescue experiments showing balance between excitation and inhibition.

claims.claim: If the sum of activity during the CP equals balance (i.e. appropriate relative amounts of each), normal physiological function is established.
claims.source: If that sum equals balance (i.e. appropriate relative amounts of each), normal physiological function is established.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the rescue experiments.

claims.claim: An imbalance in activity during the CP may lead to altered network function.
claims.source: An imbalance, however, may lead to altered network function.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the PTX-induced phenotypes.

claims.claim: parabss mutants express a hypermorphic variant of the sole Drosophila voltage-gated sodium channel (para), which makes neurons more excitable.
claims.source: parabss mutants express a hypermorphic variant of the sole Drosophila voltage-gated sodium channel (para), which makes neurons more excitable.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the parabss mutation supported by prior literature.

claims.claim: Excitation is increased at all stages of embryonic and larval development in parabss mutants, resulting in increased synchrony between aCC neurons and increased duration of electroshock-induced seizures.
claims.source: Previous work has shown that excitation is increased at all stages of embryonic and larval development, resulting in increased synchrony between aCC neurons and increased duration of electroshock-induced seizures (Marley and Baines, 2011a; Streit et al., 2016; Giachello and Baines, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: parabss recovery from electroshock was significantly longer than wild-type controls (168 ± 6.96 s, bss; 87.74 ± 3.45 s, CS; n = 50, 50; p<0.0001).
claims.source: In agreement with previous work (Giachello and Baines, 2015), parabss recovery from electroshock was significantly longer than wild-type controls (168 ± 6.96 s, bss; 87.74 ± 3.45 s, CS; n = 50, 50; p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by behavioral data and consistent with prior work.

claims.claim: The parabss seizure phenotype was rescued completely when ch neurons were stimulated during the CP at 80 dB (87.74 ± 3.45 s, CS; 94.51 ± 4.59 s, bss + 80 dB; n = 50, 50; p=0.91).
claims.source: This difference was rescued completely when ch neurons were stimulated during the CP at 80 dB (87.74 ± 3.45 s, CS; 94.51 ± 4.59 s, bss + 80 dB; n = 50, 50; p=0.91).

claims.claim: The rescue effect was reduced in a dose-dependent manner as the intensity of ch stimulation during the CP decreased (125.6 ± 5.82 s, bss + 60 dB; 144.3 ± 6.61 s, bss + 40 dB; n = 50, 50; p=0.03 for bss vs. bss + 40 dB, <0.0001 for bss vs. bss + 60 dB).
claims.source: This was the maximum strength of stimulation possible, and importantly, the effect was reduced in a dose-dependent manner as the intensity of ch stimulation during the CP decreased (125.6 ± 5.82 s, bss + 60 dB; 144.3 ± 6.61 s, bss + 40 dB; n = 50, 50; p=0.03 for bss vs. bss + 40 dB, <0.0001 for bss vs. bss + 60 dB) (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Raising parabss at 21°C reduces the duration of evoked seizure when compared to animals raised at 25°C (168 ± 6.96 s, bss 25; 113.2 ± 4.28 s, bss 21; n = 40, 50; p<0.0001).
claims.source: To test this, we raised parabss at 21°C, which reduces the duration of evoked seizure when compared to animals raised at 25°C (168 ± 6.96 s, bss 25; 113.2 ± 4.28 s, bss 21; n = 40, 50; p<0.0001).

claims.source: At 21°C, stimulating ch activity during the CP using 40 dB is sufficient to completely suppress seizure behaviour (76.24 ± 5.07 s, bss 21 + 40 dB; 86.68 ± 4.2 s, CS; n = 40, 40; p<0.44).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Ch activity at 80 dB induces a seizure phenotype in parabss raised at 21°C (130.8 ± 5.6 s, bss 21 + 80 dB; 86.68 ± 4.2 s, CS; n = 40, 40; p<0.0001).
claims.source: Notably, ch activity at 80 dB induces a seizure phenotype (130.8 ± 5.6 s, bss 21 + 80 dB; 86.68 ± 4.2 s, CS; n = 40, 40; p<0.0001), which is consistent with 80 dB ch-induced inhibition outweighing parabss-induced excitation at 21°C (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The CP integrates the excitatory and inhibitory activity to which the locomotor network is exposed using the sum (relative balance or E:I) to set key network parameters that are then 'locked in' to the mature locomotor network.
claims.source: Combined, these results support the hypothesis that the CP integrates the excitatory and inhibitory activity to which the locomotor network is exposed using the sum (relative balance or E:I) to set key network parameters that are then 'locked in' to the mature locomotor network.

claims.claim: CPs often reflect a change from spontaneous to patterned activity within neural networks.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Coulson et al., 2022.

claims.source: Early spontaneous activity that occurs prior to CP opening is predominantly excitatory and notably includes excitatory GABAergic signalling (Ben-Ari, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Ben-Ari, 2002.

claims.claim: The E:I balance is strongly biased towards excitation prior to the opening of a CP.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Allène et al., 2008.

claims.evidence: This is supported by the current experimental results and citation to prior work.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and the current experimental results.

claims.source: The second messenger calcium is likely to be involved as calcium signalling is central to activity-regulated plasticity during nervous system development, including adjustment to changing internal and external environments, as well as learning and memory (Spitzer, 2012).

results.result: Embryonic PTX exposure during the critical period increases seizure duration without affecting crawling velocity, indicating altered network robustness but preserved normal locomotor function.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 1B-C showing significant increase in electroshock recovery time (p<0.0001) but no change in crawling velocity (p=0.14). The interpretation that network robustness is altered while normal function is preserved is consistent with the data.

results.result: PTX exposure during the CP significantly increases synchronicity of motoneuron activity across segments, which is consistent with and may contribute to the observed seizure phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 are supported by GCaMP imaging data (Figure 1F) showing significant reduction in time lag between segments (p=0.05). The interpretation linking increased synchronicity to seizure phenotype is reasonable given prior literature (C30) showing similar patterns in seizure-prone mutants.

results.result: Embryonic PTX exposure shifts the E:I balance toward excitation by preferentially strengthening excitatory (A18a) over inhibitory (A31k) synaptic drive to motoneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C43 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 2) showing significant increase in A18a-mediated excitation (p=0.04) but not A31k-mediated inhibition (p=0.15), with effect size analysis (Cohen's d=1.14 vs 0.78) confirming differential changes. The conclusion of E:I imbalance is well-justified.

results.result: The increased excitatory drive following PTX exposure is mediated by postsynaptic mechanisms, as evidenced by increased mini amplitude without change in frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by voltage-clamp recordings (Figure 3) showing no change in mini frequency (p=0.11) but significant increase in amplitude (p=0.008). The interpretation of postsynaptic mechanism is consistent with established principles of synaptic physiology (C44-C45).

results.result: Using Sr2+ substitution to isolate A18a-specific minis confirms postsynaptic enhancement of excitatory transmission, with increased mini amplitude but unchanged frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 are supported by Sr2+ experiments (Figure 4) showing no change in mini frequency (p=0.97) but significant increase in amplitude (p<0.0001) specifically from A18a. The validation of the Sr2+ approach (C50) and consistency with Ca2+ results strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: PTX-induced changes in synaptic physiology occur without detectable alterations in motoneuron morphology or synapse number, suggesting changes in receptor properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by confocal microscopy data (Figure 5) showing no changes in dendritic arbor structure or Drep2 puncta number. However, C58 is speculative about receptor changes. The morphological data are solid, but the mechanistic interpretation requires further validation.

results.result: Chordotonal neuron activation during the CP, but not before or after, produces lasting effects on network function, confirming temporal specificity of the critical period.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 6B) showing significant effects only during 17-19hr AEL (p<0.0001) but not at adjacent time periods. This temporal specificity is consistent with prior work and validates the CP window.

results.result: Chordotonal neuron stimulation during the CP completely rescues PTX-induced phenotypes at behavioral, network, and cellular levels, supporting the hypothesis that CPs integrate excitatory and inhibitory activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70 are strongly supported by rescue experiments (Figure 6C-E) showing complete restoration of seizure recovery (p=0.58 vs control), synchronicity (p=0.75 vs control), and A18a input strength (p=0.53 vs control). The integration hypothesis is well-supported by these data.

results.result: Chordotonal neuron stimulation provides dose-dependent rescue of the parabss seizure phenotype, with complete rescue at 80 dB and partial rescue at lower intensities.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 7A) showing complete rescue at 80 dB (p=0.91 vs control) and graded effects at lower intensities (p<0.0001 for 60 dB, p=0.03 for 40 dB). The dose-dependent relationship is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Temperature-dependent modulation of parabss excitability combined with dose-dependent chordotonal rescue demonstrates that CPs integrate the sum of excitatory and inhibitory activity to set network parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 are supported by experiments at 21°C (Figure 7B) showing reduced baseline seizure duration and complete rescue with lower chordotonal stimulation (40 dB), while excessive stimulation (80 dB) induces seizures. This bidirectional effect strongly supports the integration hypothesis.

results.result: Baseline electrophysiological properties show some differences between PTX and control groups, but intrinsic membrane properties remain unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C38, and C41 report baseline measurements. C36 shows significant difference in baseline firing with A18a-Gal4 (p=0.03), C38 shows no difference with A31k-Gal4 (p=0.8), and C41 shows no changes in Vm, Rin, or capacitance. The data are clearly presented but the interpretation of C36 is uncertain regarding whether this reflects altered excitability or experimental variability.

results.result: Sr2+ substitution for Ca2+ promotes asynchronous vesicular release, enabling isolation of single-neuron synaptic events.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 are supported by validation experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing reduced evoked currents but increased mini frequency with Sr2+. This technique is well-established in the literature (cited) and properly validated here.

results.result: Critical periods are developmental windows during which neural circuits are particularly sensitive to activity, with changes becoming locked in and potentially contributing to neurodevelopmental disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C11-C16 provide background context supported by extensive citations to prior literature. These are well-established concepts in the field and appropriately cited. The claims accurately represent the current understanding of critical periods.

results.result: Critical periods reflect a developmental transition from spontaneous excitatory activity to patterned activity with increased inhibition, and appropriate E:I balance during CPs is necessary for normal network function.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C87 synthesize prior literature on CP mechanisms and are supported by multiple citations. The current work (C87) provides additional evidence supporting this framework. These claims accurately represent established knowledge and the contribution of the current study.

results.result: Activity during CPs may encode homeostatic set points rather than being compensated for, potentially explaining why increased excitation leads to strengthened excitatory inputs and why brief CP manipulation can rescue genetic mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C104 present a speculative mechanistic framework. While the set point hypothesis is interesting and consistent with the data, it remains speculative (explicitly noted as such in C98, C100, C104). The interpretation of the non-significant inhibitory change (C103, p=0.15) as potential homeostatic compensation is reasonable but uncertain.

results.result: The mechanism of increased mini amplitude may involve changes in cholinergic receptor subunit composition, similar to homeostatic synaptic scaling observed in mammalian visual cortex following monocular deprivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C97 discuss potential mechanisms and comparisons to mammalian systems. C92 is explicitly speculative about receptor subunit changes. C93-C95 accurately cite mammalian literature, but C96-C97 acknowledge uncertainty about whether effects are purely CP-dependent or include homeostatic compensation. Further experiments are needed to resolve these questions.

results.result: Calcium signaling, reactive oxygen species, and nitric oxide are likely involved in measuring activity levels during CPs, with potential intersections between these signaling pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C111 discuss potential molecular mechanisms. C105 and C107-C111 are supported by citations to prior work. However, C106 is explicitly speculative ('we expect'). While these signaling pathways are plausible candidates, the current study does not directly test their involvement, making this discussion speculative.

results.result: The mechanism of chordotonal neuron rescue may involve matching inhibition to excitation, or alternatively may act through effects on CPG rhythm, potentially involving a succession of developmental set points.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C124 present multiple speculative interpretations of the rescue mechanism. C115, C116, C118, C120, C122, and C124 are explicitly speculative. While C117 cites prior work on ch neuron connections, the mechanistic interpretations remain uncertain and require further experimental validation.

results.result: Multiple physiological manipulations including vibration, temperature, drugs, and optogenetics can alter network function when applied during CPs, suggesting CPs measure and integrate diverse activity influences to tune circuits to their developmental context.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C130 are supported by the current data (C126 showing vibration effects in Figure 6B) and extensive citations to prior work (C128). The synthesis that CPs integrate diverse influences (C130) is a reasonable interpretation supported by the dose-dependent rescue experiments and prior literature.

results.result: Synaptic number in Drosophila scales inversely with developmental temperature, optimizing adult movement for the developmental temperature.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C132 accurately cite prior work (Kiral et al., 2021) as supporting evidence for the broader concept that CPs tune circuits to developmental context. These claims appropriately reference prior literature to support the discussion.

results.result: The study provides novel insight into how CP activity manipulation causes lasting E:I imbalance that reduces network robustness while preserving normal function, and demonstrates that CPs tune developing networks based on integrated activity exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C137 summarize the main conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including behavioral, imaging, and electrophysiological evidence. The conclusions appropriately reflect the strength and scope of the findings.

results.result: PTX exposure during the embryonic CP increases seizure recovery time without affecting normal crawling velocity, indicating reduced network robustness but preserved baseline locomotor function.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirm these findings. Reviewer 1 states the study 'highly convincingly assayed' permanent network changes via 'prolonged recovery period following induced seizure.' Reviewer 2 notes 'compelling mechanistic insight' showing 'reduced robustness to induced seizures' while 'locomotion is not altered.' The differential effects on seizure vs. crawling are accepted without challenge.

results.result: PTX exposure during the CP increases synchronicity of motoneuron activity across segments, which is consistent with and may contribute to the seizure phenotype.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as part of the network-level changes. Reviewer 1 describes 'altered intersegmental coordination during locomotion' as a manifestation of permanent network changes. Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'increased synchronization of motor neuron networks' as one of the effects. No concerns are raised about the synchronicity measurements or their interpretation.

results.result: PTX exposure during the CP differentially strengthens excitatory (A18a) over inhibitory (A31k) synaptic inputs to motoneurons, shifting the E:I balance toward excitation without altering basic membrane properties.
results.evaluation: This is a central finding strongly endorsed by all reviewers. Reviewer 1 calls it 'a major accomplishment to track the tuning of network excitability during the CP down to the physiology of specific synapses.' Reviewer 2 describes 'very nice electrophysiology' showing these changes. Reviewer 3 states the authors 'elegantly show that picrotoxin-induced over-excitation leads to increased strength of excitatory inputs, and not loss of inhibitory inputs.' The differential effect size analysis (Cohen's d) is accepted without question.

results.result: The increased excitatory drive is mediated by postsynaptic mechanisms, as evidenced by increased mini amplitude without changes in mini frequency, both in general recordings and A18a-specific recordings using Sr2+ substitution.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support this mechanistic finding. Reviewer 1 notes 'Fine electrophysiology shows that excitatory synapse strengthening occurs postsynaptically.' Reviewer 3 specifically highlights 'Using Ca2+/Sr2+ substitutions, the authors demonstrate that synaptic connections between A18a & aCC show increased mEPSP amplitudes' as a strength. The technical approach and interpretation are accepted without criticism.

results.result: The physiological changes occur without significant alterations in dendritic morphology or synapse number, suggesting changes in receptor properties rather than structural remodeling.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these anatomical findings. Reviewer 1 states 'High quality anatomy shows that dendrite size and numbers of synaptic contacts remain unaltered.' Reviewer 2 includes this in 'very nice...imaging data that assess synaptic function and structure.' The interpretation that changes are due to receptor properties is acknowledged by Reviewer 1 as adequately addressed in the discussion, though the molecular mechanism remains unknown.

results.result: Activation of chordotonal (ch) neurons during the CP, but not before or after, increases seizure susceptibility, confirming the temporal specificity of the critical period and the role of sensory input.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this validation of the CP window. Reviewer 3 notes 'The authors confirm their previous results and show that 17-19 hours after egg laying is a critical period' as a strength. However, Reviewer 3 also requests additional controls: 'what is the effect of ch neuron stimulation alone on time lag and AP frequency?' and suggests demonstrating that 'exposure to picrotoxin at L1 or L2 do not lead to changes in induced seizure at L3' would strengthen the CP specificity claim.

results.result: Ch neuron activation during the CP completely rescues PTX-induced phenotypes at network, cellular, and synaptic levels, supporting the hypothesis that CPs integrate E:I balance to set network parameters.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the rescue is demonstrated, they express concerns about interpretation. Reviewer 1 states the experiments 'demonstrate that during the CP different forms of activity manipulation are integrated so that opposing manipulations can rescue altered setpoints.' However, Reviewer 2 notes 'the later experiments in Figures 6 and 7 designed to counteract the CP plasticity are somewhat difficult to interpret' due to unclear 'specificity of the manipulations' and questions whether 'downstream or secondary adaptations may be masking the PTX-induced plasticity.' The rescue is clear, but the mechanistic interpretation remains uncertain.

results.result: Ch neuron stimulation provides dose-dependent rescue of the parabss seizure phenotype, with the rescue level depending on both stimulation intensity and baseline excitability (temperature), supporting E:I integration during the CP.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as demonstrating dose-dependence. Reviewer 3 notes 'The authors demonstrate that the effects of over-excitation attributed to picrotoxin exposure are generalizable and also occur in bss mutant flies' as a strength. Reviewer 1 acknowledges this 'provides novel insight into how developing neural network excitability is tuned.' The dose-dependent relationship is accepted, though the mechanistic interpretation shares the uncertainties noted for the PTX rescue experiments.

results.result: Activity perturbation during the embryonic CP permanently alters locomotor circuit properties, including increased motoneuron synchronicity, altered E:I balance, reduced network robustness, and these changes can be rescued by inhibition in a dose-dependent manner, suggesting proper E:I balance during the CP is necessary for normal mature network function.
results.evaluation: This overarching conclusion is endorsed by all reviewers. The editor states this 'valuable study' provides 'novel insight into how developing neural network excitability is tuned and how it can be entrained during the CP.' Reviewer 1 calls it 'important findings' showing 'novel insight into how developing neural network excitability is tuned.' Reviewer 2 states 'this study provides an important advance in our understanding of what parameters change during CPs to calibrate network dynamics.' The core finding is strongly supported despite some mechanistic uncertainties.

results.result: The critical period for locomotor circuit development occurs specifically at 17-19 hr AEL, with activity manipulations during this window causing permanent changes, while similar manipulations at larval stages have no effect.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept the CP timing based on prior work, Reviewer 3 explicitly requests additional validation: 'The present study would benefit from demonstrating that exposure to picrotoxin at L1 or L2 do not lead to changes in induced seizure at L3. This would further the authors hypothesis of the criticality of the 17-19h AEL period.' The claim about larval stages being without effect is based on unpublished data, which weakens the evidence for temporal specificity in the current manuscript.

results.result: Background claims establishing that critical periods are sensitive developmental windows where activity-dependent changes become locked in, that aberrant activity during CPs contributes to neurodevelopmental disorders, and that Drosophila larvae provide a tractable model for studying CPs.
results.evaluation: These background claims are accepted without challenge by reviewers as established knowledge in the field. They provide context for the experimental work but are not themselves evaluated as novel findings.

results.result: Methodological and background claims about PTX mechanism, larval locomotor circuit organization, synaptic physiology principles, Sr2+ substitution technique, chordotonal neuron function, and parabss mutation characteristics.
results.evaluation: These methodological and background claims are accepted by reviewers as established knowledge or validated techniques. They support the experimental design but are not themselves novel findings being evaluated.

results.result: Discussion claims about E:I balance during development, comparison to mammalian studies, homeostatic mechanisms, set point hypothesis, and potential molecular mechanisms involving calcium, ROS, nitric oxide, and mitochondria.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the discussion as appropriate contextualization. Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'the molecular cause that underlies increased motoneuron postsynaptic responsiveness as well as the mechanism that integrates different forms of activity during the CP remain unknown. However, the discussion addresses this point adequately.' These are interpretive and speculative claims that reviewers find reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: Concluding interpretations about CP function, ch neuron mechanisms, developmental succession of set points, physiological relevance of different manipulation methods, and the broader principle that CPs tune networks based on activity exposure.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these conclusions as reasonable interpretations of the data. The editor summarizes that the study 'provides novel insight into how developing neural network excitability is tuned and how it can be entrained during the CP.' While some mechanistic details remain speculative, the overall interpretive framework is endorsed.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on C26-C28. Both evaluations find the behavioral data (seizure recovery vs. crawling velocity) well-supported and accept the interpretation of altered network robustness without functional impairment. Both rate as SUPPORTED.
Perfect agreement on C31-C33. Both evaluations accept the GCaMP imaging data showing increased synchronicity and its link to seizure phenotype. Both rate as SUPPORTED without concerns.

Strong agreement on C37-C43 regarding E:I imbalance. Both evaluations endorse the electrophysiology showing differential changes in excitation vs. inhibition. Peer review calls this 'a major accomplishment' and OpenEval confirms statistical support. Both rate as SUPPORTED. Note: Peer R3 includes C36, C38, C41 which OpenEval addresses separately in R11.

Partial overlap on baseline measurements (C36, C38, C41). OpenEval notes uncertainty about C36 interpretation (baseline firing difference), while peer review accepts these as part of the broader electrophysiology findings without specific concern. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with caveats; peer review includes in broader SUPPORTED evaluation.

Agreement on postsynaptic mechanism (C46-C48). Both evaluations accept the voltage-clamp data showing amplitude but not frequency changes. Both rate as SUPPORTED. Peer R4 also includes Sr2+ data (C51-C54) which OpenEval addresses separately in R5.

Agreement on Sr2+ validation of postsynaptic mechanism (C51-C54). Both evaluations strongly endorse this technical approach and findings. Peer review highlights this as a specific strength. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on morphological findings (C55-C58). Both evaluations accept the confocal data showing no structural changes. OpenEval notes C58 is speculative about receptor changes; peer review acknowledges molecular mechanism remains unknown but finds discussion adequate. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on CP temporal specificity (C60-C63). Both evaluations accept the 17-19hr AEL window validation. However, peer review requests additional controls (L1/L2 exposure experiments) to strengthen CP specificity claims. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED; peer review rates SUPPORTED but with request for additional validation.

Divergence on rescue interpretation (C64-C70). OpenEval finds rescue experiments strongly support the integration hypothesis (SUPPORTED). Peer review acknowledges rescue is demonstrated but expresses concerns about mechanistic interpretation, noting experiments are 'somewhat difficult to interpret' due to unclear specificity and potential secondary adaptations (UNCERTAIN).

Agreement on dose-dependent effects (C73-C75). Both evaluations accept the graded rescue with different sound intensities. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED; peer review accepts findings as demonstrating dose-dependence (SUPPORTED), though mechanistic interpretation shares uncertainties noted for PTX rescue.

Agreement on bidirectional effects at 21°C (C76-C80). Both evaluations accept the data showing reduced baseline seizures and bidirectional effects of stimulation. OpenEval finds this strongly supports integration hypothesis (SUPPORTED); peer review accepts as demonstrating generalizability (SUPPORTED).

Agreement on Sr2+ technique validation (C49-C50). Both evaluations accept this as established methodology properly validated. Both rate as SUPPORTED. Peer R12 groups this with other methodological claims not specifically evaluated by OpenEval.

Agreement on background/context claims (C1-C3, C11-C16). Both evaluations accept these as well-established concepts appropriately cited. Both rate as SUPPORTED. These provide context rather than novel findings.

Agreement on CP mechanism synthesis (C81-C87). Both evaluations accept these claims as accurate representation of prior literature and current contribution. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED; peer review accepts as appropriate contextualization (SUPPORTED).
